passages.t: One family in ten, chosen by lot
passages.happening:
‘Now the leaders of the people settled in Jerusalem, and the rest of the people cast lots to bring one out of ten to live in the holy city of Jerusalem, while the remaining nine were to dwell in their own towns’ (verse 1).

‘And the people blessed all the men who volunteered to live in Jerusalem’ (verse 2).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 7 left Jerusalem walled but nearly empty: ‘Now the city was large and spacious, but there were few people in it’ (7:4). Nehemiah began then to enroll the people, but the story paused for the reading of the law, the confession and the pledge. Now it picks up where chapter 7 left off.

Jerusalem in the Persian period was far smaller than it had been before 587 or 586 BC. Many returnees preferred to live in the towns and villages where they had land, since farming was their living, and Jerusalem had few houses and little economic life apart from the temple. Moving into the capital meant giving up property and security for the sake of the city.

Casting lots was a common way in Israel to settle a decision no one wanted to make by preference, and it was understood that God directed the result. The land itself had first been divided by lot. Using lots took the choice out of the hands of the powerful. And taking one in ten echoes the tithe, the tenth given to God; some interpreters see the people giving a tenth of their families to the holy city in the same spirit.

The volunteers are honored. The verb behind volunteered is the one used for freewill offerings, given without being forced. The people treat their move as a kind of offering.
passages.later: The wisdom of Proverbs says what the people believed about the lot: ‘The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD’ (Proverbs 16:33). And the prophets had promised that Jerusalem would be called holy again: ‘Put on your garments of splendor, O Jerusalem, holy city’ (Isaiah 52:1).
passages.asks: Some went to the city because the lot fell on them, and some went because they chose to. Ask where you have been sent somewhere you did not choose, and how you have lived there. And ask what you might give up, as the volunteers did, for the sake of a place God cares about.

passages.t: Those who lived in the holy city
passages.happening:
The chapter lists the leading residents of Jerusalem. From Judah, the descendants of Perez, 468 men of valor (verse 6). From Benjamin, 928 (verse 8). Then the priests, 822 who did the work of the temple, with others under their own leaders (verses 10-14); the Levites, among them two leaders who oversaw ‘the work outside the house of God’ (verse 16) and Mattaniah, a descendant of Asaph, ‘who led in thanksgiving and prayer’ (verse 17). ‘The Levites in the holy city totaled 284’ (verse 18). The gatekeepers, 172 men, kept watch at the gates (verse 19).

The rest of Israel lived in the villages of Judah, each on his own land (verse 20). The temple servants lived on the hill of Ophel (verse 21). The overseer of the Levites was Uzzi, one of Asaph's descendants, the singers ‘in charge of the service of the house of God’ (verse 22). There was a command from the king about the singers (verse 23), and Pethahiah ‘was the king’s agent in every matter concerning the people’ (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
The list is arranged by groups: Judah, Benjamin, the priests, the Levites, the gatekeepers, and notes on the temple servants, the overseer of the Levites and the king's agent. Its numbers give a sense of how small the city was. And the holy city is named at the start and in the middle (verses 1 and 18), marking what the whole arrangement is for.

A close parallel to this list stands in 1 Chronicles 9, with many of the same names and some differences, which suggests that both drew on temple and city records of the period.

Verse 23 mentions a command from the king about the singers. Interpreters are divided over whether this means the Persian king, who might have granted support to the temple staff, as Artaxerxes did in Ezra 7, or David, who is credited elsewhere with organizing the singers. Pethahiah, the king's agent, is most often taken to be a Jewish official who represented the people's affairs at the Persian court.
passages.later: The same kind of list of Jerusalem's residents stands in Chronicles: ‘Now the first to resettle their own property in their cities were Israelites, priests, Levites, and temple servants’ (1 Chronicles 9:2).
passages.asks: The holy city needed priests and singers, but also gatekeepers, overseers and men of valor. Ask what part you play in the life of God's people, and whether you count it as holy. And ask who leads you in thanksgiving and prayer, as Mattaniah led his city.

passages.t: The towns of Judah and Benjamin
passages.happening: The rest of the people live in towns and villages. Some of the people of Judah live in Kiriath-arba, in Beersheba, in Ziklag, Lachish and Azekah and their villages. ‘So they settled from Beersheba all the way to the Valley of Hinnom’ (verse 30). The people of Benjamin, from Geba on, live in Michmash, Bethel, Anathoth, Ramah, Lod, Ono and other towns (verses 31-35). And some divisions of the Levites of Judah settle in Benjamin (verse 36).
passages.hearers:
The towns include places with deep roots in Israel's history. Kiriath-arba is the old name of Hebron. Beersheba lay in the far south. Bethel, Anathoth and Ramah belong to the old land of Benjamin.

From Beersheba to the Valley of Hinnom echoes older descriptions of Judah's reach, from the far south to the valley beside Jerusalem. Some scholars think the list describes where Jews actually lived, including areas beyond the official borders of the Persian province. Others think it expresses the community's claim to the old tribal land. These notes take no side, and they make no claim about any border today.
passages.later: The land had first been shared out by lot, as the people now chose who would live in Jerusalem: ‘Their inheritance was assigned by lot for the nine and a half tribes, as the LORD had commanded through Moses’ (Joshua 14:2).
passages.asks: Most of the people stayed in their towns, and the list names them too. Ask whether you think of faithfulness as something that happens only at the center, or in ordinary towns as well. And ask what it would mean to be faithful in your own village.
